notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: The red strip wraps over the top, all the way round the back and partly the front, often with a thin yellow or white reflector. These bollards are unique.

notes.subject: plate
notes.text: White plates with black text that look mostly white through the blur; custom plates can show blue or black sides.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: The usual pole is concrete with one long indent most of the way up and small silver possum guards; wooden round poles and holey poles also occur.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Give-way signs have a white border and red text, and give-way triangles are often painted on the road at intersections.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Most direction and warning signs sit on white posts; warning signs are yellow diamonds.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Blue street signs with white text are by far the most common, especially in rural areas; the neighbour almost never has them.

notes.subject: line
notes.text: Edge lines are normally white, with yellow dashed ones in populated areas; centre lines are a dashed white line or unbroken double yellow.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Black-on-yellow chevrons have a thin black border; white-on-black ones are very rare.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Green direction signs show state highway numbers in a red crest; brown signs point to landmarks.

notes.subject: street
notes.text: Most paved roads have bridge markers: a white one with the highway in a red crest and a yellow one naming the river or bridge.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Ferns commonly grow in forested areas.

notes.subject: other
notes.text: Phone numbers are 7 digits with a 2-digit area code; numbers starting 02 are mobiles.

notes.subject: sign
notes.text: Two-digit state highways are numbered sequentially from north to south; single-digit ones run through large parts of the country.

notes.subject: car
notes.text: A car with a white and blue front is mostly on the northern island; a blurred white-blue-white pattern car is mainly on the southern island and around and north of Auckland.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: The West Coast and part of Tasman have temperate rainforest, rugged terrain and dark compact greenery from heavy rain.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Flatter Southland and Otago have a cold climate with sloping alpine hills and stunted vegetation; flax in long neat rows suggests Southland.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Waikato and Northland have a drier climate and rolling hills; gravel roads and Generation 2 coverage are common in Northland.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Dry golden grassy hills mark Hawke's Bay; vineyards are common there and in Marlborough.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Bright sandy cliffs are common in central Manawatū-Whanganui and appear in parts of Taranaki, Waikato and a road into Hawke's Bay.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: The Southern Alps around Queenstown have many glacial lakes with teal, clear water.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: A smooth-sloped, pointed, often snowy volcano stands over flat surroundings and is visible from afar.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Very flat plains with tall hedge and tree rows and mountains in the distance to the west.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Very tall hedges and green-netted fruit farms are common around Tauranga.

notes.subject: vegetation
notes.text: Corn is almost exclusively found on the northern island.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Many Marlborough poles have a long, square, olive-brown possum guard beside the usual short silver ones.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Southland poles often have a long cylindrical silver possum guard; square concrete poles without an indent and holey poles are also common there.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: A yellow cow-tag-like tag is on most Gisborne poles.

notes.subject: pole
notes.text: Poles near Timaru often carry a tall rectangle of orange paint reading DANGER LIVE WIRES.

notes.subject: bollard
notes.text: A bollard with a green stripe is common in southern Canterbury; one with a black stripe is common in the capital region, especially older Generation 3.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: The capital is very hilly.

notes.subject: coverage
notes.text: The southern island's tiny neighbour has coverage only around one settlement and a bay full of small boats, Generation 3 only.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Tongariro National Park has low volcanic vegetation, and the dark, nearly bare terrain of Mount Ruapehu around the ski village.

notes.subject: architecture
notes.text: Coverage from 2012 in the big southern-island city shows damaged roads, cut-off driveways and districts with houses removed.

notes.subject: landscape
notes.text: Densely forested mountains rising from the water in the north of Marlborough, almost only Generation 4.

notes.subject: vegetation
notes.text: Cabbage trees, yellow-flowered gorse, small groves of cone-shaped pines and flax, with off-centre crossbars on poles.
